certainty_reasoning: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), names him at printed 96, 100, 102 and 109 - as 'Elephant', a later addition to the household, an alcoholic Ives kept when the Goddard daughters left over his drinking, and joint inheritor of the Adelaide Road house with Bloodworth. Cook's account of the household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date, but no passage naming Saunders in Ives's own voice appears in any source read, so the attestation is the historian's rather than a participant's.
date_label: Ives's household, later years - undated in the sources.
summary: Stanley Saunders - 'Elephant' among the household nicknames - lived with George Ives at Adelaide Road in Ives's later years. Cook names him as a household member, as joint inheritor of the house and its contents with Harold Bloodworth, and as the man Ives kept when the Goddard daughters left over his drinking. Cook characterises the Adelaide Road relationships as having 'possibly started sexually' before becoming platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. No first-person characterisation by either man survives in any source read; Ives's diaries at the Harry Ransom Center are where one would be.

sources.quote: He referred to his housemates affectionately but patronisingly with infantilising nicknames (Cubby, Pug, Kit, Elephant - Therese was Chooki) and also frequently as his 'children'. … 'My children all laugh at me', he complained, 'but they have not the responsibility of running a house with six or eight people in it; all to be milked for'.
sources.context: Cook, at printed 100, listing the pet names Ives used for the Adelaide Road household and then quoting Ives's diary (vol. 85, 1 August 1923, p. 46, per Cook's endnote 27). Elided between the two sentences: Cook's report that Ives was their 'old bird' and that they teased him to his face for being 'a stingy old b'.
sources.supports: The closest this record can come to Ives characterizing Saunders in his own voice, and the limit is worth stating exactly. Cook records that 'Elephant' was a name Ives himself used, and Ives's diary then names the household collectively as 'my children' - so the relationship Ives claimed with the men he lived with is paternal, proprietary and affectionate at once. But the naming is collective: Ives nowhere names Saunders or 'Elephant' in any first-person passage Cook prints, and Cook never dates Elephant's arrival, so whether Saunders was among the 'six or eight people' of the 1923 entry is not established. Ives's testimony reaching us through Cook, from Diary vol. 85. See the documented-absence note below.

sources.quote: He moved from the countryside into London, lived in London for most of his life, mostly in a suburban house in North London, where he lived with a succession of younger men who sometimes stayed for just a few years, sometimes they stayed for decades.
sources.context: Brian Lewis, spoken in a National Humanities Center podcast interview about Ives; ASR transcript, wording may vary slightly from the audio. Establishes the household pattern only - Lewis names no individuals here
sources.supports: Context only: the documented pattern of younger men in Ives's household, within which the leads place Saunders
sources.provenance: Discovery & Inspiration - Brian Lewis, "George Cecil Ives and the Transformation of Discourses on Sexuality"

sources.context: Saunders ('Elephant') as a named member and reputed lover in Ives's later household. No first-person passage about Saunders exists in either Cook book: the words 'Saunders' and 'Elephant' occur only in Cook's own narration (printed 96, 100, 102, 109-110, 110), never in a quotation from Ives; the chapter's endnotes (printed 125-131) cite the diary by volume and date for some twenty passages, none attached to a sentence naming Saunders. Cook's endnote 22, the source for Ives choosing Elephant over the Goddard daughters, credits Brian Lewis by personal communication with no archival citation. The Cook (2003) text mirror likewise shows neither name in the Ives material.
sources.supports: The existence, dates, and character of the Ives-Saunders relationship. Everything the record currently holds about this pair is Cook narrating, or Lewis speaking to Cook. No Ives diary entry alluding to a romantic relationship with Saunders has been located yet.

sources.quote: Though Ives' relationships with the other men at Adelaide Road possibly started sexually, they seem quickly to have become platonic - even though he continued to sleep with them from time to time.
sources.context: Cook's summary characterization of the Adelaide Road household relationships
sources.supports: Cook's own careful reading: a possible sexual beginning, a platonic settling, continued bed-sharing throughout.

sources.quote: The two men he was living with - Harold Bloodworth and Stanley Saunders (Pug and Elephant) - were left the Adelaide Road house and contents; Tilly Hayes was next in line to inherit after them.
sources.context: Cook, on the provisions of Ives's will (made October 1939 per Cook's text; dated 1 December 1939 per his endnote 80)
sources.supports: First citable source naming Saunders: co-heir with Bloodworth to the Adelaide Road house and contents.
sources.provenance: PDF pp. 120-121; the sentence runs across the page break.

sources.quote: They could no longer put up with the Elephant's alcoholism, and left to open a shop using money Ives had settled on their father. Ives effectively chose Elephant over them - even though, as a teetotaller, his drinking was a source of considerable angst for him too.
sources.context: Cook, on the Goddard daughters' departure from Adelaide Road in the early 1940s
sources.supports: Saunders's alcoholism, and Cook's judgement that Ives preferred keeping Saunders to keeping the Goddard daughters. Note this is Cook's interpretive gloss on an outcome, not a recorded declaration by Ives; and Cook's endnote 22 credits the observation to Brian Lewis (personal communication), with no archival citation behind it.

sources.quote: Therese and Adele clearly had little time for Elephant (Stanley), and though their parents were very attached to Ives, it is unclear whether they understood themselves to be more staff than family, or more family than staff.
sources.context: Cook, on how the members of the Adelaide Road household may have understood one another
sources.supports: Confirms 'Elephant' = Stanley Saunders from a second page, and records the friction with the Goddard daughters that Cook says drove them out.
